questions.q: Name the three broad categories of washing methods taught in Class 12 Home Science and give one example of a fabric suitable for each category.
questions.a: The three categories are: (1) Friction washing — e.g., cotton kurta; (2) Machine washing — e.g., polyester blend shirt; (3) Special techniques — e.g., woolen sweater. A wrong answer that lists "dry cleaning" as a category reveals confusion between washing (aqueous) and dry cleaning (solvent-based) processes, which are covered in a separate node (c12_hs_cbse_14_010).

questions.q: Explain why beating with a wooden stick is suitable for heavy cotton bedsheets but would damage a silk saree. Use the terms "fibre strength", "yarn structure", and "mechanical action" in your explanation.
questions.a: Beating applies high-impact mechanical action that cotton’s high fibre strength and tight plain weave can withstand, dislodging dirt from the yarn structure. Silk has lower wet strength, a smooth filament yarn structure, and is prone to yarn slippage and fibre rupture under impact. A wrong answer that says "silk is delicate" without linking to fibre properties shows surface-level memorisation rather than understanding the structure-property relationship taught in Class 11 (c11_hs_cbse_05_005, c11_hs_cbse_05_006).

questions.q: A student wants to wash a moderately soiled polyester-cotton blend shirt in a fully automatic front-load washing machine. Select the appropriate wash cycle (cotton, synthetic, delicate, wool) and justify your choice based on the machine’s tumble action and the fabric’s properties.
questions.a: Choose the "synthetic" cycle. Front-load tumble action lifts and drops garments, creating moderate mechanical action. Polyester-cotton blend has good wet strength and dimensional stability but can crease excessively under high agitation and high spin speeds; the synthetic cycle uses lower agitation and spin than cotton cycle. A wrong answer choosing "cotton" cycle indicates the student does not understand that cycle names correspond to agitation intensity, not just fibre content, and overlooks creasing tendency of blends.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the mechanical action of a top-load agitator machine and a front-load tumble machine. Which is generally gentler on fabrics and why? Relate your answer to the direction of force applied on the fabric.
questions.a: Top-load agitator: central vertical post creates strong directional water currents and fabric-to-fabric rubbing, applying shear forces tangentially. Front-load tumble: horizontal drum rotates, lifting fabric and dropping it under gravity, applying primarily compressive and mild shear forces. Front-load is gentler because gravity-driven drop creates lower peak forces than the continuous aggressive rubbing of an agitator. A wrong answer claiming agitator is gentler because "it uses water" confuses water volume with mechanical action intensity.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "For a heavily embroidered georgette saree, suction washing is the best method because it removes dirt without any mechanical friction." Identify the correct and incorrect parts of this statement.
questions.a: Correct: Suction washing (using a suction washer or manual suction device) minimizes mechanical friction and is suitable for delicate, embroidered fabrics. Incorrect: "without any mechanical friction" — suction creates a pressure differential that pulls detergent solution through the fabric, which still exerts a mild hydrodynamic shear force; also, heavily soiled areas may need gentle hand kneading. A wrong answer accepting the statement fully shows inability to critically evaluate "frictionless" claims and overlooks that some mechanical action is always present in aqueous cleaning.

questions.q: Design a step-by-step washing procedure for a mixed load containing: (a) white cotton socks, (b) coloured polyester T-shirts, (c) a woolen cardigan. Specify the method for each item, the sequence if done manually, and how you would adapt if only a semi-automatic top-load machine is available.
questions.a: Manual sequence: 1) Woolen cardigan first — knead-and-squeeze in lukewarm water with mild detergent, rinse, roll in towel. 2) Coloured polyester T-shirts — hand friction wash in warm water, rinse. 3) White cotton socks — heavy hand friction/brush with hot water and bleach, rinse. Semi-automatic adaptation: Run woolen cardigan separately on "delicate" (if available) or hand-wash only; wash polyester T-shirts on "normal" cycle; wash cotton socks on "heavy" cycle with hot water. A poor answer that puts all in one machine load reveals failure to apply sorting principles (node c12_hs_cbse_14_004) and fibre-specific needs.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Washing methods refer to the ______ techniques used to remove dirt and stains from fabrics through the combined action of water, detergent, and physical agitation; the three main categories are friction washing (hand rubbing, brush, beating), machine washing (agitator, tumble, pulsator), and special techniques (kneading, squeezing, suction washing) for delicate fabrics.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have three ______: a heavily soiled cotton kurta, a delicate silk saree, and a woolen sweater.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) classify a given fabric into the correct washing method category with justification, (2) explain the working principle of at least two types of washing machines, and (3) demonstrate the steps of a special technique like kneading-and-squeezing for a woolen garment.
